strengths: Assessed primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with an accompanying method; the paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: vision-language-action manipulation when target objects move rather than remain static.

Introduces DOMINO, a large-scale dynamic manipulation benchmark with 35 tasks across 5 robot embodiments, over 110K/117K expert trajectories, canonical and domain-randomized settings, and a three-level dynamic difficulty taxonomy controlled by a scalar coefficient alpha.

Provides systematic closed-loop evaluation of many strong VLA baselines, including OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, RDT-1B, pi0, pi0.5, pi0-FAST, VLA-Adapter, InternVLA-M1, Isaac-GR00T, and ACT, showing severe static-to-dynamic degradation and providing useful findings.

Proposes PUMA, a dynamics-aware VLA that combines historical optical-flow encoding with auxiliary object-centric future feature prediction. The design is simple, adds negligible inference overhead, and matches pi0.5 latency while improving success rate.

Ablations support the design choices: explicit historical optical flow, auxiliary future prediction, and longer prediction horizons improve performance, while raw historical frames degrade it, suggesting representation matters more than merely adding past frames.

Includes real-world validation on an AgileX Piper platform with five dynamic tasks, reporting 42% average SR for PUMA versus 24% for pi0.5 and lower for ACT/RDT, plus simulation-to-real LoRA adaptation.

Provides additional analyses on cross-level transfer, dynamic coefficient generalization, data scaling, co-training with static data, failure modes, and limitations, which strengthens the empirical case.
Implementation details, data formats, caching strategies, training hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols are described in the supplementary material, supporting reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: The benchmark's realism is limited by a stop-on-contact simplification: once the gripper contacts a moving object, autonomous motion stops. This removes important post-contact dynamics, contact-induced object motion, deformable-object effects, and multi-object interactions that are central to real dynamic manipulation, so the claim of generalizable dynamic manipulation is somewhat overstated.

Most main experiments use only Level 1 predictable low-order dynamics with alpha=0.1. Higher levels, alpha out-of-distribution settings, and cross-level transfer are evaluated only on a 10-task subset, and real-world experiments use string-driven linear trajectories. The full hierarchical benchmark is therefore not thoroughly validated.

PUMA's methodological novelty is moderate: it combines historical optical flow, auxiliary future-feature prediction, and world queries, which are related to existing temporal/world-model VLA approaches. The contribution is more a well-engineered integration than a fundamentally new algorithm.

Absolute success rates remain low (e.g., 17.20% average SR on 35 tasks), with many tasks near zero. The 6.3% absolute improvement over the strongest baseline is meaningful but still leaves substantial room before the method can be considered a reliable dynamic manipulation solution.
No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported. Given low success rates and stochastic dynamic environments, the statistical significance of the reported gains is unclear.

The proposed Manipulation Score and route-completion metric are not fully convincing for moving targets: using the final object position in the progress ratio can be ill-defined when the target continues moving, and the penalty multipliers (0.5, 0.8) appear ad hoc.

Several baselines are reimplemented with a Qwen3-VL backbone rather than using official checkpoints, and some recent history-aware or world-model VLA methods are only discussed or compared in the appendix. This limits the strength of the state-of-the-art comparison.

The dataset release plan, code, and exact benchmark access details are not explicitly stated in the manuscript. Reproducibility depends on RoboTwin 2.0, SAPIEN, GroundingDINO, SAM2, and DINO components whose behavior may affect dataset generation and supervision quality.

The paper labels the work as generalizable dynamic manipulation, but the evidence supports a useful benchmark and a modest dynamics-aware policy rather than a fully general solution. The limitations section acknowledges some of this, but the main claims remain broader than the validated scope.

strengths: Introduces DOMINO, a large-scale dynamic manipulation dataset/benchmark with 35 tasks, 117K trajectories, five embodiments, hierarchical difficulty levels, and multi-dimensional metrics, which addresses an underexplored area.
Provides extensive baseline evaluations of many VLA models in static versus dynamic settings, including per-task breakdowns and ablations, giving a useful empirical snapshot of current limitations.

PUMA combines historical optical-flow cues with auxiliary object-centric future-feature prediction in a reasonable and relatively low-inference-overhead design, improving SR/MS over several baselines.
Includes real-world transfer experiments on an AgileX Piper platform and shows promising gains over ACT, RDT-1B, and pi0.5, albeit on a small task set.
Supplementary material provides useful implementation details, data-generation pipeline descriptions, caching strategies, and additional ablations.
weaknesses: The stop-on-contact simplification is a serious issue: dynamic objects are kinematic and stop moving once contact is detected, so many so-called dynamic tracking tasks do not actually require continuous tracking during manipulation. This undermines the central claim of generalizable dynamic manipulation.

Pre-contact object motion is not physically coupled to the scene, limiting realism: targets can move as kinematic bodies until contact, which weakens the benchmark as a test of real dynamic interaction.

The main experiments focus on Level 1 dynamics with alpha=0.1; Level 2/3 are evaluated only on a 10-task subset, and real-world experiments cover only five Level 1 tasks, so the claimed hierarchical and generalizable dynamic benchmark is not fully supported.

Missing direct comparisons with recent dynamic- or world-model-aware VLAs (e.g., DreamVLA, WorldVLA, ReconVLA, ContextVLA in the main text) makes the state-of-the-art claim less convincing; most baselines are general VLAs, not dynamic-manipulation specialists.

Absolute success rates remain very low (PUMA 17.2% SR on DOMINO@0.1), and the paper reports no confidence intervals or statistical significance, making the 6.3% absolute gain modest and hard to assess.
The proposed Manipulation Score and Route Completion metrics are not well justified; penalty factors appear arbitrary, and the metric behavior is inconsistent between static and dynamic settings.

Some presentation issues reduce clarity: Table 1 average entries are confusing (e.g., deltas formatted ambiguously), supplementary section numbering is malformed, and several claims are stronger than the evidence provided.
Reproducibility is uncertain: there is no clear statement that DOMINO data/code will be released, and key details such as baseline training budgets/backbone sizes are under-specified.

The PUMA method is largely an engineering combination of historical optical flow and auxiliary future-feature prediction; novelty is incremental relative to existing temporal/world-model VLA approaches.

strengths: Introduces DOMINO, a large-scale dynamic manipulation benchmark with 117K expert trajectories, 35 tasks, 5 robot embodiments, three difficulty levels, and multi-dimensional metrics; this is a valuable resource for embodied AI and dynamic manipulation research.

Systematically evaluates existing VLA models in dynamic environments and clearly exposes their severe performance degradation relative to static settings, providing useful benchmark findings and motivation.

Proposes PUMA, which combines historical optical-flow context with object-centric future prediction via world queries; the method is technically reasonable and achieves consistent gains over strong baselines on DOMINO@0.1 (e.g., 17.20% vs 10.86% SR).

Includes informative ablations showing that explicit optical-flow history is better than raw-frame history, future prediction improves performance, and prediction horizon matters; latency analysis shows the dynamic-awareness modules add only modest overhead.
Provides real-world validation on an AgileX Piper platform for five dynamic tasks, demonstrating sim-to-real transfer via LoRA adaptation and supporting the practical relevance of the approach.
weaknesses: The generalization claims are broader than the evidence: main comparisons are mostly on Level 1 predictable low-order dynamics, while Level 2/3 results are only on a 10-task subset and remain very low (e.g., 4.6% SR at Level 3). Cross-embodiment generalization is not evaluated despite five embodiments in the dataset.

The claim that dynamic training transfers to static tasks is not convincingly supported by the reported experiments. In the detailed dynamic-to-static results, average performance is generally lower than static-to-static performance for several baselines, and the observed gains appear task-specific rather than broad.

The data generation pipeline uses kinematic target motion and stops the object upon contact, which simplifies post-contact dynamics and may limit how well the benchmark captures real-world dynamic manipulation challenges such as deformable objects, multi-object interaction, and contact-rich dynamics.

The main evaluation is restricted to a clean setting with the Aloha-AgileX robot, and the real-world experiments use only five tasks with 20 trials each; stronger evidence would require more diverse robots, randomized visual conditions, and per-task variance reporting.

Absolute success rates remain low: PUMA reaches only 17.2% SR on Level 1 DOMINO@0.1, and even the real-world average is 42% on selected tasks. This is appropriate for a hard benchmark but limits claims about solving generalizable dynamic manipulation.

Reproducibility of the benchmark and method would be strengthened by an explicit public-release plan, licensing, and access details for DOMINO and PUMA; the manuscript does not clearly state these in the main text.
